runs.text: do com papel algũa couſa, ou com peça fi-

lines.note: The initial do completes grudando from f173: haritate means covering something completely by pasting paper or fine material onto it. The scan supports com, not dom; the latter disrupts the Portuguese construction.
Completes fina, qualifying peça in the preceding line. This is the end of the covering/pasting definition, not a separate entry.
Hari-tsukai is the use of a needle or lancet, here specifically bloodletting in animals. The example repeats the headword across the line break.
Together with Fari- this gives hari-tsukai wo itasu, to perform that bloodletting. Itasu supplies the action verb; this is not an independent tsukai entry.

runs.text: Hũa maneira de portas de paſta de

lines.note: Haritsuke here denotes pasted paper panels, not the unrelated crucifixion sense of the same modern reading. The long Portuguese architectural description governs the interpretation.

runs.text: papel pegadas no parede com ſuas faſquias ao

lines.note: The panels are pasted to the wall and have surrounding narrow wooden strips; fasquias is the key construction term. The scan appears to read no parede, despite the grammatical expectation na parede; the visible o is retained. Ao continues into redor below.

runs.text: redor de pao vruxado de preto, pera que res-

lines.note: The surrounding wood is black-lacquered. Vruxado is a Portuguese-shaped expression related to urushi; res- belongs to respondão on the next line, meaning that the panels match the other doors.

runs.text: pondão às de mais portas de papel que eſtão no

lines.note: Continues respondão: the fixed panels correspond to the other paper doors in the room. The final no is visually problematic: only an n-like form is clearly visible before the rule. Retained provisionally rather than treating the grammatical expectation as proof of a visible o.

runs.text: Zaxiqi, & ſe correm, ou abrem, & fechão.

lines.note: Zashiki names the room within the Portuguese explanation; the movable panels slide, open, and close. The scan has an uppercase Z and italic type, both preserved without imposing the more usual roman styling of Japanese insertions.
Hariyaburu means to tear or break, matching rasgar/quebrar. The inflectional abbreviations are kept as printed, including utta; they are not silently modernized from the kana guide.
Harō is the Sino-Japanese word for waves, explained by native nami and Portuguese ondas. This is unrelated to the following haru, spring.
Haru means spring. The printed Portuguese separates prima vera; it is not joined to modern primavera in Level 1.
Harubaru is treated here as an adverb of extended duration, glossed ha muito. Its familiar spatial sense should not overwrite this temporal Portuguese definition.
Harubaru no modifies something long or extended. The following examples apply that length to a detour and a road.
Harubaru no mawari is a long circuit or detour. Portuguese rodeo confirms mawari as going around, rather than an unrelated homophone.
Harubaru no michi means a long road. Neither Japanese nor Portuguese is supplied with an editorial final period where the scan does not clearly show one.
Harubi is a horse's girth. Cinta and silha both identify a fastening strap, not the saddle itself.

runs.text: Buraco que eſta na ſella por

lines.note: Harubi-dōshi names the saddle opening through which the girth passes. The printed douoxi represents the voiced compound form of tōshi; the following line completes its function.

runs.text: onde paſſa a ſilha do cauallo.

lines.note: Completes por onde: through which the horse's girth passes. This confirms that the headword denotes an opening rather than another strap.
Haruka denotes great distance. The Portuguese is a direct spatial gloss, unlike the temporal use of harubaru earlier in the column.
Harukaze is spring wind: haru plus kaze, with je representing ze. It is not a derivative of haruka despite its neighboring position.
Haruka na and haruka no are alternative modifying forms for something distant. The isolated l is the alternative marker, not part of Japanese.
Haruka no michi exemplifies a distant or long road. Longe completes the adjective definition before the example begins.
Completes the road example as long or distant. Comprido concerns extent, whereas distante can describe remoteness.
Haruka ni is the corresponding adverbial form. The short line supplies only the grammatical label, borrowing its meaning from the preceding entry.
Harukesa nominalizes remoteness or distance. The P label is visibly upright here; its typeface is preserved separately from the italic Adu above.

runs.text: Bichos de ſeda da prima vera.

lines.note: Haruko denotes spring silkworms. Bichos de seda establishes the insect sense; ko should not automatically be interpreted as a human child.

runs.text: Filho nacido de cão, ou animal ſeme-

lines.note: Harugo, with voiced g, denotes a spring-born puppy or the young of a similar animal. The Portuguese distinguishes it from the silkworm entry above.
Completes semelhante and specifies spring as the time of birth. The seasonal phrase belongs to the offspring definition, not to an independent entry.

runs.text: Cauallo que na prima vera brinca,

lines.note: Harugoma is a horse frisking in spring. Goma is the voiced compound form related to koma; the next line adds its sexual excitement.
Cio gives an alternative description of the horse as being in heat. The definition concerns a springtime horse, not necessarily a wooden hobbyhorse.
Harusame means spring rain. The Portuguese seasonal definition excludes the later food sense of the same Japanese word.
Hasami is the instrument, scissors or pincers. Troquez broadens the sense beyond cutting blades to implements that grip between two parts.
Hasami/hasamu is now the verb, to grip or hold something between two things. The abbreviated past ǒda preserves the historical contracted form rather than modern hasanda.

runs.text: couſa entre duas como quem toma com tiſouras.

lines.note: Completes the verb definition with the comparison of taking something in scissors. The shared concept is holding between opposing surfaces, not necessarily cutting.
Sakana wo hasamu means taking food between chopsticks. The Portuguese reuses Sacana as an embedded Japanese noun; the broader food/accompaniment sense is possible, so it need not be narrowed to fish.
Faxis is Portuguese-pluralized hashi, chopsticks, within the explanation. A separate Japanese example begins kirumono nado wo take: clothing or similar things held in bamboo.
Take ni hasamu completes the previous example: insert the garment across a split bamboo or between sticks. The locative ni identifies what holds it.

runs.text: hũa cana aberta pello meo, ou ẽtre duas canas,

lines.note: The Portuguese distinguishes a single cane split down the middle from two separate canes. Both arrangements explain the same Japanese gripping action.
After completing the stick example, the dictionary marks a metaphorical use: uma ippiki wo hasamu, keeping a horse to ride. Ippiki is the animal counter, not a separate noun.

runs.text: Ter caualo em que hum poſſa caual-

lines.note: Completes hasamu and explains having a horse on which one can ride. The physical image of gripping/straddling underlies the metaphorical use indicated above.
Cavalgar ends across the break. The Japanese example then describes a person of sufficient standing or means to keep one horse; fi- continues as fito.
Completes fito de gozaru, the polite predicate describing that person. Bastante pera ter expresses sufficiency of means or status, not physical size.

runs.text: hum cauallo, ou caualgar em cauallo. ¶

lines.note: Ends the horse example and begins another Japanese phrase with Fa-. This fragment must be read with nauo below, not as an independent word.

Joined to Fa- above, the phrase reads hana wo hasōde iru. The Portuguese describes remaining reserved or dissembling rather than responding; the idiomatic connection with literal hana is uncertain. The scan supports the transmitted phrase, so no more familiar idiom is substituted.

runs.text: ſponder, nem ter deuer com o que lhe perguntão.

lines.note: Completes responder and describes not engaging with what one is asked. The historical wording ter deuer com is retained rather than recast as a modern idiom.
Ashi wo hasōde hito wo itamuru means hurting a person by clamping the feet. The next column supplies the torture apparatus; contracted hasōde belongs to hasamu, not a different verb.

runs.text: mento a alguem entalando lhe os pès entre ta-

lines.note: Tormento continues from column 1. The example describes torture by clamping someone's feet between boards; pès is feet, with its printed accent retained.

Completes taboas, followed by paos, wooden sticks. The scan then gives Troſ- before quiar below: a further meaning of hasamu is to shear. Both the long final letter and division mark are visible, not merely supplied from spelling.
Completes trosquiar, to shear or clip. This short line belongs to the extra hasamu sense, not to the following carrying-box entry.

runs.text: Caixa que ſe leua fechada cõ algũ

lines.note: Hasamibako is a closed carrying box with clothing inside. The next line explains how it is carried on a pole.

runs.text: veſtido dentro às coſtas atraueſada em hũ pao.

lines.note: The box is carried across the back or shoulders on a wooden pole. Atraueſada qualifies the carrying arrangement, not the clothing's condition.

runs.text: Cana em que leuão às costas al-

lines.note: Hasamidake is the bamboo used to carry a garment or another object on the shoulders. Dake is voiced take in the compound.
Completes algum and names the load: clothing or another object. This supports the carrying-pole interpretation rather than a botanical species.
Hasami-ita are boards between which material is folded and pressed. The next line specifies Japanese pieces or fabrics.
Completes the paired actions dobrão/apertão, folding and pressing. The definition is of a two-board apparatus rather than a single tabletop.

runs.text: Couſa que ſe aferra cõ troquez,

lines.note: Hasamimono is something grasped with pincers or between sticks. The following text narrows one common application to food taken with chopsticks.
Two sticks provide an alternative to pincers. Signi- continues into fica; the ensuing special sense is an extension of the general gripping definition.

runs.text: fica a Sacana que ſe toma com as Faxis.

lines.note: Sacana and Faxis are embedded Japanese food and chopstick terms within Portuguese syntax. Faxis has a Portuguese plural ending; neither word is a fresh headword here.

runs.text: ¶ Item, Hum papel que poem por aluo me-

lines.note: A second sense is a paper target, placed or held in a support. Aluo means target here, not simply something white.

Completes metido: the paper is inserted into split bamboo. The middle of rachado is worn, but the established reading fits the visible ascenders and the physical description; it is not replaced on shape alone.
Hasamikiri is cutting with scissors or pincers. The compact conjugation is retained as printed; its u abbreviation is not expanded in the diplomatic line.
Adds pincers or similar cutting implements to the scissors gloss. It concludes the preceding verb rather than introducing a new tool entry.
Hasamitateru is putting or fixing something between two supports. The tate element can also contribute an upright orientation, illustrated below.

runs.text: couſa entre duas apertada. Item, Por al-

lines.note: The first gloss emphasizes a tight fit between two things. Item begins a second, upright placement sense without creating a new headword.

runs.text: gũa couſa aleuantada entre duas como adaga

lines.note: Describes something standing between two objects, illustrated by a dagger. Aleuantada accounts for the tate element of the Japanese compound.
The dagger stands between two tatami mats. Tatamis is an embedded Japanese noun with Portuguese plural s; the joined entredous is retained as printed.

Hasami-orosu means cutting or shearing off. The abbreviated past looks like oita in the scan; although morphology suggests oroshita, the diplomatic form is not expanded or repaired solely on that expectation.

Amari no senkata nasa ni describes extreme helplessness. The object should semantically be hakuhatsu, white hair, confirmed by cabelos brancos below. However, enlargement shows a short t-like letter in facutatuo, not a clearly intact f: the visible reading is retained and the likely intended facufatuo is recorded here rather than silently substituted.

Completes hasami-orosu; the source label Feiq. cites book 4 of the Heike. The scan shows the label and its period in roman type, followed by italic Lib.; the Portuguese describes cutting the hair in helplessness.

Completes poder and explicitly identifies the cut material as white hair. This is strong evidence for the intended Japanese hakuhatsu, but cannot repair an apparently defective printed letter by itself.
Hasan is explained by sakazuki wo kubaru, distributing or directing a drinking cup. This ceremonial sense is distinct from the accounting and brokerage homonyms below.

runs.text: dirigir o Sacazzuqi a alguem. Vt,

lines.note: Sacazzuqi is the cup embedded in the Portuguese sentence. Go- begins the honorific form gohasan in the ensuing Japanese example.

runs.text: A quem quereis que ſe de o Sa-

lines.note: Gohasan are is interpreted by the dictionary as asking to whom the cup should be given. The Portuguese cup name begins Sa- at the right edge and continues below.
Completes the Japanese loanword Sacazzuqi within the Portuguese explanation. Its scan type is italic despite the preceding occurrence being upright; the local distinction is preserved.

runs.text: O interceder, ou aueriguar opreço en-

lines.note: This hasan is mediation or settling a price. Portuguese interceder and the following buyer/seller context distinguish it from both cup distribution and clearing an abacus.

runs.text: tre os que comprão, & vẽdem. Vt,

lines.note: Completes entre and identifies the parties as buyers and sellers. Hasan begins the example whose suru follows on the next line.
Hasan suru is acting as a broker. Corretor supplies the occupational sense and should not be confused with correcting written text.
Here hasan is clearing or undoing a completed reckoning, explained by hasuru. The following reference to counters establishes the abacus sense rather than modern financial bankruptcy alone.

runs.text: cõtas depois de concluidas, ou baralhar os ten-

lines.note: The reckoning has already been completed; its counters are then mixed or cleared. Ten- continues into tentos, the calculating counters, not attempts.
Completes tentos das contas. This physical resetting of counters explains hasan in its arithmetic sense.
Hasō is a broken window, directly glossed yabureta mado. The P label and its point appear upright; the headword's open long vowel is not changed to the pronunciation of the following hason.
Hason means damage or breaking; yabure sonzuru is the native explanatory phrase. The Portuguese applies it specifically to a vessel breaking or being wrecked.
Completes nauio and gives fune ga hason shita as the example. Fune is the vessel and ga marks the subject.
Shita completes the Japanese past predicate. The vessel broke or was lost; perdeu-se here concerns shipwreck, not merely misplacing an object.

runs.text: Primeiro dia da oitaua lũa a que ſe

lines.note: Hassaku is the first day of the eighth lunar month. Oitaua lũa identifies a calendrical month, not the eighth visible moon of a night.
Completes the statement that this day is celebrated in Japan. The brief line belongs to hassaku and supplies its social significance.
Hassai na mono describes a talkative woman in this definition. The uncommon adjective is supported by NINJAL's matching headword; it is not normalized to a more familiar modern insult.
Muito modifies talking or chattering on the previous line. It concludes the description of excessive speech, not the arithmetic entry below.
Hassan denotes division in arithmetic, with a cross-reference to Gisan. The joined diuidirnas is retained; this is distinct from single-s hasan, clearing a calculation.

runs.text: Oito eſtados que teue a vida de

lines.note: Hassō denotes eight stages of the Buddha's life. The scan shows an additional short s after the long one, matching NINJAL's Fassǒ; omitting it incorrectly merges this entry with hasō, a broken window. Xaca begins an embedded Japanese name in upright type.
Completes Xaca-Bup, Shaka Buddha, from the previous line. This short fragment is body text in the definition of the eight stages, not a catchword or a new entry.

Hassoku is setting out, explained as ashi wo okosu, lifting or setting the feet in motion. The scan supports uo, the object marker, not no; the Portuguese specifies a noble person's departure for war.
Completes the departure-for-war definition and identifies its subject as a noble person. The separate Fa at the lower right is the catchword, not part of this sentence.
